The Story of Sanjayant Muni

Bowing to the lotus feet of the blessed Jina, bestower of happiness, I write the story of the monk Sanjayant, who illuminated the path of right austerity.

To the west of Mount Sumeru, in the land of Videh, there lies a country called Gandhamalini. Its chief city is Vitshokpur. At the time of our story, its king was Vaijayant, and his queen was Bhavya. They had two sons, named Sanjayant and Jayant.

One day, a bolt of lightning struck and killed King Vaijayant's prized royal elephant. Witnessing this sudden destruction, the king felt a powerful wave of renunciation arise in his heart. He resolved to give up his kingdom and summoned both his sons to entrust them with the burden of rule. But the brothers replied, "Father, a kingdom only increases worldly entanglement. Rather than happiness, it will bring us suffering. Is this not the very reason you are leaving it? Because it is harmful, a cause of sin? Therefore, we believe that wise men — those who care for the welfare of their souls — should not take upon themselves the burden of ruling, which destroys their natural peace. For this reason, we do not think it right to accept the throne. Instead, we wish to become monks along with you and attend to the welfare of our souls."

Vaijayant did not press them further. Respecting their wishes, he permitted them to take monkhood. He entrusted the kingdom to Sanjayant's son, also named Vaijayant, and himself became a wandering ascetic. Both brothers also took initiation as monks.

As a monk, the elder Vaijayant practised intense austerities and bore every hardship with patience. At last, through the fire of meditation, he destroyed all destructive karmas and attained keval jnan — the omniscient knowledge that illuminates all worlds. At that moment, gods descended from heaven to celebrate his attainment of knowledge.

When the younger brother Jayant beheld the celestial splendour and divine beauty of the visiting gods, he made a wish: "I have performed so much austerity. I desire that through its power, I may receive such beauty and such grandeur in my next birth." And so it came to pass. His wish bore fruit. At the end of his life, he was reborn as Dharnendra — a powerful celestial being.

But the elder brother Sanjayant followed a different path entirely. He had no wish for worldly or heavenly rewards. He began to observe increasingly severe fasts — fasting for fifteen days at a stretch, then for an entire month, caring nothing for hunger or thirst. He bore the twenty-two types of hardship (parishaha) that a Jain monk is called upon to endure: hunger, thirst, cold, heat, insect bites, illness, pain, discomfort, and many more.

His body grew thin and frail, but his spirit burned ever brighter. He sat in deep meditation for days on end, unmoved by any external circumstance. His austerity was so extraordinary that it became legendary among both monks and laypeople. People came from distant lands merely to catch a glimpse of this great ascetic.

Through this unparalleled penance, Sanjayant purified his soul of all karmic matter. In time, he too attained keval jnan, and at the end of his earthly life, he achieved moksha — the supreme liberation from which there is no return to the cycle of birth and death.

The story of Sanjayant Muni teaches us the true meaning of right austerity. It is not performed for the sake of any reward — neither earthly power nor heavenly pleasure. It is performed solely for the purification of the soul. And when austerity is combined with right faith and right knowledge, it becomes the fire that burns away every chain of karma and sets the soul forever free.
